These generic overrides are for when the user knows what the element is going to be and needs access to special properties or methods on the HTML element. It is probably going to be pretty rare, but may be required in rare circumstances (maybe a hacked file upload that requires an `HTMLInputElement` type.

The fallback for all generic overrides is `HTMLElement` which contains all the generic methods and properties. Also the `Subject` returned by all Element selectors is a `JQuery` object which helps to normalize a lot of calls.

A way of getting the right element without using a generic would be to use the `.filter` method:

```ts
cy.get('.input') // HTMLElement since we can't infer type
  .filter('input') // HTMLInputElement since 'input' is a keyof match
  .then($input => {
    $el // $ExpectType JQuery<HTMLInputElement>
  })
```

That would also always make sure you have an `<input>` or else the test will fail before it gets there. I prefer this over generic overrides since overriding generics is basically overriding the type system (possible runtime error in that case)

I wonder if, given that info, that should be the way to get a specific element type? I don't like seeing generics in non-library code - it is just too easy to misuse.

Generics would still be required in areas we can't infer based on input (like fixture contents or results from a `.as`).
We can't narrow the type down much with a `.not`. I'm not even sure a generic should be used here. `HTMLElement` is what all elements would have in common. I think I'll remove the generic from this.

I added `ChainableArray<Subject>` to properly capture types for `.each` and `.spread` and theoretically any Command that is meant to work on arrays. Without this, `.each` and `.spread` would be forced to resort to `any` for parameters, putting more type burden on the application author.

The `Omit` part basically takes the whole `Chainable` interface and removes some keys ('and', 'as', etc in this case). I'm defining the `ChainableArray` interface to be the same as `Chainable` except a few methods are replaced with different type definitions. Without knowing much about Node.js streams or what is actually replaced here, I wonder how are replacements handled that fall over the chunk boundary?

`tail`, `replacement`, and `chunk` are all JS strings that consist only of complete Unicode graphemes (thanks to `utf8-stream` and `grapheme-splitter`), so by concatting/replacing with them there should not be any character boundary issues.

I'm not talking about splitting Unicode graphemes on the chunk boundaries, I'm talking about the string replacement here. If the matching string has the first half in one chunk and the second half in the next, the `tail.replace(pattern, replacement)` won't find it. 'chunk boundary friendliness' is one of the features of the original _replacestream_ library.

If you check out [`replacestream`'s options](https://github.com/eugeneware/replacestream#list-of-options), the `maxMatchLen` option controls the maximum length of the buffer to do replacements in. Here, `tail` is that buffer. This should work across cross-chunk boundaries in a similar way to `replacestream` by holding a buffer of `maxTailLength` size back.

It feels like part of the responsibly of a loader is to provide a scrim over the appropriate content. This can either be the entire viewport (fullscreen) or any element (non-fullscreen). However, in both cases, it prevents the user from taking action until after the loader has completed. This seems like the intended purpose of a loading screen/loader.

I am not suggesting to bake into `Loader` a scrim. The concept of a scrim stands on its own. However, we can leverage a Scrim (ui-block, etc.) and compose it within `Loader`.

Specifically, my suggestions are:
- compose Loader with a scrim (or ui-block; doesn't have be named Scrim)
- full screen loaders show a scrim the entire viewport
- non-full screen loaders show a scrim over their parent consumer
    - if we simply do not need a non-full screen loader, then consider naming this `FullScreenLoader` instead. If we come back in the future with a need for a non-fullscreen version then it can simply compose the `FullScreenLoader` within it.

Note: I would defer the non-fullscreen loader if possible; as it is more complicated in terms of implementation.

Edit: It appears like there is at least [one usage](https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/pull/3268/files#diff-2f9b8415c2aa516569e9ba1e934f198cR60) of a non-fullscreen loader.

It's not the *most* important thing, but still, in this PR we have a chance to...

* maintain a consistent user experience,
* have well-defined retry behavior around an error-prone section of code,
* avoid introducing new dependencies since we already have this functionality in createRetryingSocket,
* and reduce confusion/technical debt around this code section instead of adding new complexity and external libraries that developers have to understand

If we don't do it before this PR gets merged, it just becomes even more tech debt, and this code is only a few months old so we should try to keep it in nice shape for as long as possible.

I can implement it if you like since I already know the APIs involved, just let me know.

Be my guest and change it.
I would prefer using off the shelf 3rd party libs for this, since they are well tested. I also don't find the argument for introducing technical debt convincing. We will do more stuff in the retry function:
- connect to socket
- `CRI.List`
- check if the list contains the blank page

If the check fails, we are going to go ... and connect back to the socket? What if we just need more time ... to get `CRI.List` to query the tabs AFTER the connection? Will we get into a loop where we are not solving the problem? 

Right now it seems to me the retries are split where they need to be and are isolated.

You raise a good point re: reconnecting to the socket on each retry, that probably shouldn't happen.

I still think that it's important to preserve the retry messaging. Otherwise the error experience will look like this:

```
Retrying 20/33...
Retrying 21/33...
Failed to connect to browser
```

...then the user is left head-scratching, "why didn't it just retry like it said it was going to?" and we'll have to fix it later on...

So maybe we can keep pRetry and then move the "warning message" into a function that keeps track of how many times it's retried, so we can use it in both places when a retry occurs.

```html
<shadow-root>
```

```js
 	cy.get('bar')
```

No, you still need to pass the option to get `bar` without enabling it at a higher level (test config, cypress.json, etc). The option is only in effect for the duration of the command.

So `cy.get('bar', { includeShadowDom: true })` outside the `within` could traverse through multiple shadow boundaries and find `bar`. However, `cy.within` does not persist the `includeShadowDom` behavior. It acts as it normally does and scopes queries inside so if there was another `bar` outside `foo`, it would not also be in the result of `cy.get('bar')`.

Windows's NTFS and FAT32 filesystems prohibit using `:` inside of a filename, which is why this separator character was chosen:

* https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/naming-a-file#naming-conventions
* https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filename#Comparison_of_filename_limitations

However, in Linux ext4 filesystem, it is perfectly fine to create a filename with a colon in it:

```
➜ ~ echo "foo" > test:file
➜ ~ cat test:file
foo
```

I think this reinforces the idea that this feature should be Windows-only, so we can *avoid* having to create additional logic to make paths containing colons still work.
